transcript:
Meeting: Northstar Healthcare - Redwood Private POC scoping (VPC networking / DNS / TLS)
Recorded: 2025-06-26 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein (SE), Colin O'Donnell (SE), Fatima Noor (Solutions/Regulated)
Northstar Healthcare: Priya Nair (Platform Eng), James Carter (Network Eng), Elena Ruiz (Security), Matt Hwang (Cloud Infra)

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Northstar is exploring a Redwood Private POC in AWS with strict egress controls.
- Key risks are DNS resolution behavior, TLS/cert management, and required AWS endpoints for a private EKS-based install.
- Redwood will share alpha Terraform modules + a reference architecture and provide a checklist of required endpoints and installer prerequisites.

Topics
1) POC goals & timeline
2) VPC topology (subnets, NAT/egress, endpoints)
3) DNS (private hosted zones, Route53 resolver, split-horizon)
4) TLS/cert chain (ACM vs internal PKI)
5) Logging & audit trail defaults
6) Next steps

Action items (auto)
- Share Terraform draft and reference architecture (Redwood)
- Confirm CIDR/region/egress policy (Northstar)
- Follow-up deep dive on DNS/TLS (Both)

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we’re recording. Cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Markus from Redwood. I’ve got Colin and Fatima with me. Goal today is POC scoping for Private deployment, specifically VPC stuff, DNS, TLS, and then timelines. Sound good?

[00:18] Priya Nair: Yep, sounds good.

[00:20] James Carter: Yeah.

[00:21] Elena Ruiz: Works.

[00:23] Markus Klein: Awesome. Quick round of intros just in case. I’m Solutions Engineering, I’ll be your point. Colin’s been on a bunch of the pilots. Fatima focuses on regulated and, like, on-prem futures.

[00:36] Colin O'Donnell: Hey everyone.

[00:37] Fatima Noor: Hi.

[00:39] Priya Nair: Priya, platform engineering. I’ll be shepherding this internally.

[00:43] James Carter: James, network. I own VPC patterns and connectivity.

[00:47] Elena Ruiz: Elena, security and risk. I’m mostly here to make sure we don’t accidentally create a hole in the side of the ship.

[00:54] Matt Hwang: Matt, cloud infra. I do EKS and shared services.

[00:58] Markus Klein: Great. So, Priya, maybe start with what you’re trying to prove with the POC? Is it model quality, or is it more “can we run this in our network constraints”?

[01:10] Priya Nair: It’s mostly the second. We already did some bench with hosted APIs, like, Bedrock and Azure, but the blocker for prod is we need it inside our AWS account, and we have pretty strict egress policies. We want to validate you can deploy in a private VPC, we can do audit logging, and that we’re not going to have a six-month networking project.

[01:33] Markus Klein: That makes sense. That aligns with what we’ve seen. When you say strict egress, are we talking “no internet gateway, period” or “egress via NAT but with controls” or “only via proxy”?

[01:45] James Carter: Ideally no direct internet. We can do NAT gateways in some accounts, but it’s heavily reviewed. The preference is VPC endpoints wherever possible, and anything else goes through an outbound proxy that does inspection.

[02:00] Colin O'Donnell: Got it. So basically private subnets, and either no NAT or NAT-only-as-exception.

[02:05] James Carter: Yeah.

[02:06] Markus Klein: And timeline wise, what are you aiming for? Like, when do you want a yes/no on this POC?

[02:14] Priya Nair: We want something running in July. If we can start next week with terraform and get the cluster up mid-July, then do a two-week functional test, that’d be ideal.

[02:28] Markus Klein: That’s aggressive but doable if we keep scope tight.

[02:31] Elena Ruiz: And assuming we don’t get stuck on DNS. That’s usually where we get stuck.

[02:35] Markus Klein: Yep. Let’s talk about the network and DNS path early then.

[02:40] Matt Hwang: For context, we run EKS with private API endpoints typically. Control plane is private. Nodes in private subnets. We use internal load balancers.

[02:50] Colin O'Donnell: Great. That’s consistent with our “standard private” reference architecture.

[02:55] Markus Klein: Okay. I’ll share a high-level of what we recommend for alpha. We’ve been building an opinionated set of Terraform modules that stand up the VPC footprint with “Redwood-validated” defaults: VPC + subnets, routing, endpoints, flow logs, security group patterns, and an IAM scaffold for the installer role. It’s not a full app install; it’s like foundational.

[03:18] Priya Nair: That would be great because we don’t want to invent our own best practices here.

[03:22] James Carter: What are the assumptions baked in? Like number of AZs, NAT per AZ, that kind of thing.

[03:28] Colin O'Donnell: In the current draft, default is 2 or 3 AZs, private subnets per AZ for nodes, and then optional public subnets if you choose NAT. We corrected some earlier assumptions on NAT mapping—there was a “NAT per AZ” expectation that didn’t always hold, so now it’s more explicit.

[03:48] James Carter: Good, because we often do centralized egress.

[03:52] Markus Klein: We can support centralized egress as an extension point. Alpha is opinionated but not rigid. The key thing is: for a zero-public-everything approach, we rely on VPC endpoints heavily.

[04:04] Matt Hwang: Can you list which endpoints are “required” versus “nice to have”?

[04:09] Colin O'Donnell: For the installer and day-0 cluster boot, the pain points we’ve seen: ECR (both api and dkr), S3 (gateway endpoint), STS, CloudWatch Logs if you’re shipping logs there, and often EC2 and ELB for provisioning. Depending on how you pull charts/images, also KMS if you’re doing envelope encryption.

[04:31] James Carter: Wait, you need internet for anything? Like pulling public images?

[04:34] Colin O'Donnell: Ideally no. We can use private ECR repos and mirrored artifacts. But if you’re pulling from public registries, you either need NAT/proxy, or you pre-stage images. Our installer can detect missing endpoints now and will warn early—like, “missing ECR endpoints” is a common failure mode.

[04:54] Priya Nair: That’s good. We’ve had Helm installs fail late and it’s painful.

[04:59] Elena Ruiz: On endpoints: we’re okay enabling them, but private DNS is sometimes tricky. Our DNS is kind of split: on-prem authoritative, with forwarders into AWS.

[05:10] Markus Klein: Perfect segue. James/Elena, can you describe DNS topology? Are you using Route 53 resolver endpoints today?

[05:18] James Carter: Yes. We have inbound and outbound resolver endpoints in a shared services VPC. Then we attach VPCs via Transit Gateway. The app VPC forwards to on-prem for corp zones, and on-prem forwards to AWS for some private zones.

[05:36] Elena Ruiz: And we have controls about which teams can create private hosted zones. There’s governance.

[05:42] Markus Klein: Understood. For a private deployment, main DNS concerns are:
1) Private DNS for interface endpoints (ECR, STS, etc.) so the AWS service names resolve internally.
2) Internal service discovery for the cluster ingress endpoint(s).
3) If you need to reach on-prem resources (like HSM, SIEM, internal auth), ensuring forwarders are stable.

[06:05] Colin O'Donnell: We’ve also seen intermittent DNS issues inside private subnets if resolver rules aren’t consistent across VPCs or if there’s a weird caching layer. Not sure if that applies to you.

[06:15] James Carter: We’ve seen that, yeah. Usually it’s a combination of resolver rules and endpoint private DNS toggles.

[06:21] Matt Hwang: Also CoreDNS configs in EKS if nodes can’t reach resolver.

[06:25] Markus Klein: Exactly. So for POC, we want to keep it simple. Ideally the POC VPC has the necessary resolver rules, and we enable private DNS on the interface endpoints unless your governance prohibits it. If it does, we can do explicit private hosted zone records, but that’s more manual.

[06:44] Elena Ruiz: We can enable private DNS, but it has to go through review. We need a list and justification.

[06:50] Colin O'Donnell: We can provide that. We have a checklist with “why”: without private DNS, ECR pulls can fail because the endpoint name resolves to public IPs.

[07:01] Priya Nair: Great. What about TLS? We’re going to need internal-only endpoints, and our clients will likely call through a private integration layer.

[07:10] Markus Klein: For TLS, typical pattern is internal NLB/ALB, certificate from either ACM Private CA or your internal PKI. Do you use ACM PCA?

[07:20] Matt Hwang: We don’t use ACM PCA widely. We have an internal CA on-prem. We can issue certs but it’s a process.

[07:28] Elena Ruiz: We also have requirements around cert chain and rotation. If you can integrate with our PKI, that’s ideal.

[07:36] Fatima Noor: That’s common in healthcare. For alpha, we try not to force one way. We can accept a customer-provided cert for the internal load balancer endpoint. The installer/Helm charts support referencing a secret with the cert and key. The part we need to align on is: what is the hostname and where does DNS live.

[07:56] James Carter: Hostnames would be in our internal zone, like something.northstar.health, and resolution is via on-prem forwarders.

[08:06] Colin O'Donnell: That works. We just need to confirm the direction: do you want the LB to be addressed by that hostname from within VPC only, or also from on-prem via VPN/Direct Connect?

[08:17] James Carter: For POC, within VPC only. Longer term, we might need on-prem connectivity because some apps run in our data center.

[08:27] Markus Klein: Perfect. For POC then, we can keep connectivity simple and not bake in Direct Connect assumptions. Our Terraform modules have placeholders/outputs to integrate with VPN/DX later.

[08:39] Priya Nair: So basically: create VPC, subnets, endpoints, EKS, then your installer goes on top.

[08:45] Markus Klein: Yes. And to be transparent: our alpha Terraform suite handles the VPC and foundational plumbing; EKS can be your existing module or we can reference a standard. The Redwood Private installer is what validates and deploys the actual Redwood stack.

[08:59] Matt Hwang: We have our own EKS module. I’d prefer to use that.

[09:03] Colin O'Donnell: Totally fine. We’ll just need specific outputs: subnet IDs, cluster security groups, VPC ID, endpoints info, and sometimes the route table IDs if we need to validate egress patterns.

[09:17] James Carter: On security groups: do you have an “allow all egress” requirement for nodes?

[09:22] Colin O'Donnell: Not “allow all”, but nodes need to reach AWS endpoints and whatever internal dependencies you have. We provide an opinionated SG pattern: restrict ingress, and for egress either allow to VPC CIDR + endpoint SGs. There’s always a tension between least-privilege and operability.

[09:40] Elena Ruiz: We prefer least-privilege, but we don’t want constant break/fix.

[09:45] Markus Klein: Our default is “secure by default but not brittle.” In alpha we’ll document the recommended deltas. For POC, we can start slightly more permissive on egress and then tighten once it’s stable.

[10:00] Priya Nair: That’s acceptable.

[10:02] Markus Klein: Let’s talk logging and audit. Elena, what do you need to see for the POC to be acceptable?

[10:09] Elena Ruiz: Flow logs are usually required. And application logs need to get to Splunk. We can do CloudWatch logs but retention and access need to be locked down.

[10:19] Colin O'Donnell: Our default is enabling VPC Flow Logs and letting you choose destination: CloudWatch or S3. Some customers prefer customer-owned S3 buckets with lifecycle policies, then ship to SIEM.

[10:32] Elena Ruiz: S3 is often easier for us. But we need encryption and KMS keys.

[10:37] Fatima Noor: Yep. We can recommend a KMS key for log buckets, and ensure policies restrict access. We also can provide the IAM boundary approach we use for installer roles.

[10:48] James Carter: Wait, installer role—does your installer assume it can create networking resources?

[10:53] Markus Klein: Good question. We’re separating concerns. Terraform is for networking. Installer role is scoped to what it needs for deploying the application layer (EKS resources, maybe some IAM, depending). We can support permission boundaries so it can’t go wild.

[11:10] Elena Ruiz: That will be important.

[11:12] Markus Klein: Okay. I’m going to check POC environment details. Are you planning to do this in a dedicated AWS account or shared?

[11:19] Priya Nair: Dedicated account within our org, but we have shared services attached.

[11:24] Matt Hwang: Region likely us-east-1.

[11:27] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Any constraints on AZ count? Some orgs only allow 2.

[11:32] James Carter: Two AZs is fine.

[11:34] Markus Klein: Great. CIDR ranges already allocated?

[11:38] Priya Nair: Not yet, but we can do /20 or /19, probably.

[11:43] James Carter: We’ll confirm. It depends on TGW attachments.

[11:47] Markus Klein: Cool. Now, a key question: do you require EKS private endpoint only? You said yes typically.

[11:54] Matt Hwang: For POC, yes. We can do private API endpoint and no public.

[12:00] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Just note: some tooling needs access to the API endpoint from wherever you run kubectl/installer. We usually run the installer from inside the VPC (like a bastion or a CI runner). Is that feasible?

[12:13] Priya Nair: Yes, we can run from a self-hosted runner in the account.

[12:18] Elena Ruiz: As long as there’s no inbound from internet.

[12:21] Markus Klein: Great.

[12:23] (crosstalk)

[12:24] James Carter: How do you handle outbound calls from the application itself? Like does Redwood need to call home for license checks or telemetry?

[12:32] Markus Klein: Good question. For Private, we support operating without outbound connectivity to Redwood. There are optional update checks, but for regulated customers we assume restricted egress. We’ll be explicit about what’s required and what’s optional.

[12:46] Elena Ruiz: That’s important. We have a “no phone home” default.

[12:50] Fatima Noor: Understood.

[12:52] Markus Klein: Okay, let’s zoom into endpoints again. Colin, can you speak to “minimum set” for a zero-egress install?

[13:00] Colin O'Donnell: For AWS services: ECR api + dkr, S3 gateway, STS, CloudWatch Logs (if used), EC2, ELB, Autoscaling. Sometimes EKS endpoint is inside, but that’s not a VPC endpoint; it’s the cluster itself. Also, if you use SSM for node management, you need SSM endpoints.

[13:23] Matt Hwang: We do use SSM.

[13:25] Colin O'Donnell: Then add SSM, EC2 messages, SSM messages.

[13:30] James Carter: And KMS.

[13:31] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, KMS if you’re doing encrypted volumes or log buckets.

[13:36] Elena Ruiz: We are.

[13:38] Markus Klein: Great, we’ll include those.

[13:41] Priya Nair: Can your Terraform modules create those endpoints? Or do we do it?

[13:46] Markus Klein: Our alpha modules include an endpoints module that can create them with defaults, and you can toggle which ones. But if you have a shared services pattern that centralizes endpoints, we can adapt.

[13:58] James Carter: We do not centralize endpoints. Usually per VPC.

[14:02] Markus Klein: Great, then it’s straightforward.

[14:05] Elena Ruiz: DNS again: if we enable private DNS for endpoints, does that interfere with our resolver rules?

[14:12] Colin O'Donnell: Generally no, it just means the standard AWS service DNS names resolve to private IPs within the VPC. But if you have a resolver rule that forwards “amazonaws.com” somewhere else, that can conflict. We should check your rules.

[14:28] James Carter: We do have some broad rules, yeah.

[14:31] Markus Klein: Okay, action item: can you send us a sanitized view of your resolver rules for that account/VPC? Even just “these suffixes forward where.”

[14:41] James Carter: We can.

[14:43] Priya Nair: I’ll coordinate that.

[14:45] Markus Klein: Great.

[14:47] Matt Hwang: For TLS, if we provide a cert, where does it terminate? At NLB? Or inside the pods?

[14:54] Colin O'Donnell: Usually at the ingress (like NGINX or Envoy) or the AWS load balancer controller depending. Many customers terminate at the ALB/NLB and re-encrypt internally, or terminate at ingress and do TLS there. We can support either. For simplicity, terminate at the internal ALB with your cert.

[15:16] Elena Ruiz: Are you okay with TLS 1.2 minimum and specific ciphers?

[15:20] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We can align on your baseline.

[15:24] Fatima Noor: Also, if you have mTLS requirements between internal callers and the endpoint, we need to confirm early. That adds complexity.

[15:34] Elena Ruiz: For POC, no mTLS, but production maybe.

[15:38] Markus Klein: Okay.

[15:40] Priya Nair: Let’s talk about what we need from you to start next week. You mentioned Terraform module draft and architecture doc.

[15:48] Markus Klein: Yep. We’ll send:
- Reference architecture for AWS private VPC deployment (EKS assumed)
- Terraform module draft (alpha) and example tfvars
- A deployment guide that’s basically prerequisites -> apply -> validation -> handoff to installer

[16:07] Colin O'Donnell: And I’ll include the endpoint/DNS checklist and a note about installer preflight checks that detect missing ECR endpoints, etc.

[16:16] Priya Nair: Great.

[16:18] Markus Klein: On your side, we’ll need:
- AWS account ready and permissions for your Terraform pipeline
- Proposed CIDR and subnet sizing
- Decision on NAT/proxy vs “endpoints only” for POC
- DNS plan (private hosted zone vs your corp zone)
- TLS plan (who issues cert and what hostname)

[16:42] James Carter: NAT/proxy decision is basically “proxy only” for exceptions. But we’d like to try endpoints only.

[16:50] Colin O'Donnell: Endpoints-only is possible, just more strict about artifact sources. We’ll need to mirror any images you’d otherwise pull from public.

[17:01] Matt Hwang: Can you provide a list of images?

[17:04] Colin O'Donnell: We can provide a list or we can do it during install planning. It depends on which components you enable.

[17:12] Markus Klein: For POC, we should define a minimal feature set to reduce dependencies. Probably: one model, basic chat/generation endpoint, and logging.

[17:23] Priya Nair: Agreed.

[17:25] Elena Ruiz: Also audit logging.

[17:27] Markus Klein: Yep.

[17:29] (brief pause)

[17:31] Markus Klein: Any procurement/legal constraints that would block a POC? Sometimes healthcare has BAAs, etc.

[17:38] Elena Ruiz: For POC in our account with no PHI, it’s okay. But we still need security review sign-off. That’s why we’re here.

[17:47] Markus Klein: Understood.

[17:49] Priya Nair: What about on-prem future? We’re not doing it now, but we want to make sure we’re not painted into a corner.

[17:56] Fatima Noor: The architecture is similar: private networking, internal DNS, internal certs, and strict logging. Our private deployment product has an on-prem option, but for alpha Terraform modules we’re focused on AWS VPC. The key is we keep interfaces stable: you’ll have a consistent API endpoint and observability story.

[18:14] Priya Nair: Okay.

[18:16] James Carter: One more thing: do you require IPv6?

[18:19] Colin O'Donnell: No, IPv4 is fine.

[18:22] James Carter: Good.

[18:24] Markus Klein: Let’s make sure we capture risks. From our side, the main POC risks are:
- DNS conflicts with private DNS endpoints and resolver rules
- ECR pulls / artifact access without NAT
- Cert issuance lead time

[18:44] Elena Ruiz: Add logging approvals.

[18:46] Markus Klein: Yep.

[18:48] Priya Nair: So next meeting should be DNS/TLS deep dive.

[18:52] Markus Klein: Agree. We’ll schedule a 60-min next week. We can bring Victor (networking) if needed, but maybe not unless we hit complexity.

[19:03] James Carter: That would help.

[19:05] Markus Klein: Okay, we’ll tentatively include him.

[19:08] Colin O'Donnell: Before we wrap, I want to confirm: do you allow interface endpoints in all private subnets? Sometimes customers only allow in a specific subnet tier.

[19:18] James Carter: We can allow in private subnets, but they must have security groups locked down.

[19:23] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Our modules attach SGs to endpoints and restrict inbound to VPC CIDR or specific SGs.

[19:30] Elena Ruiz: Make sure it’s not “0.0.0.0/0” anywhere.

[19:33] Colin O'Donnell: Yep.

[19:35] Markus Klein: Cool. Priya, does July still feel realistic given what we discussed?

[19:40] Priya Nair: If you send docs tomorrow and we can get network review early next week, yes.

[19:46] Matt Hwang: We can stand up EKS quickly once VPC is approved.

[19:50] Markus Klein: Great.

[19:52] Elena Ruiz: One request: label clearly what’s alpha and what’s “supported.” We don’t want to rely on something that will change weekly.

[20:00] Markus Klein: Totally fair. We’ll recommend pinning module versions and we’ll be explicit about what might change. Alpha means we may iterate, but we’ll coordinate upgrades.

[20:12] Priya Nair: Okay.

[20:14] Markus Klein: Alright, I’m going to recap next steps.

Recap / Next steps
- Redwood (Markus) will send Terraform module draft + example tfvars + AWS private VPC reference architecture by Friday.
- Redwood (Colin) will send endpoint + DNS prerequisite checklist and installer preflight notes.
- Redwood (Fatima) will send security posture note: logging defaults and IAM boundary approach for installer execution role.
- Northstar (Priya/James) will confirm CIDR, region, AZ count, and share a sanitized resolver rule summary.
- Northstar (Elena) will confirm logging destinations/retention and any restrictions on CloudWatch.
- Both teams will schedule a DNS/TLS-focused follow-up (60 minutes) next week.

[20:58] Markus Klein: Did I miss anything?

[21:00] James Carter: No, that covers it.

[21:02] Elena Ruiz: All good.

[21:03] Priya Nair: Thanks.

[21:05] Markus Klein: Great. Thanks everyone.

(Note: Fireflies transcript truncated in some sections; minor speaker attribution errors may exist.)
